hints: Focus on what happens to the C=C double bond in propene when it undergoes addition polymerisation.
Notice that every carbon in the backbone chain ends up with four single bonds, so identify its hybridisation and shape.
Connect that tetrahedral carbon shape to its characteristic bond angle to decide what every C-C-C angle must be.
walkthrough:
**Write what polymerisation does**

Think of propene as $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_3$. In addition polymerisation the pi bond breaks and each monomer joins by two new single bonds to neighbours.

Polymer repeat unit:
$$-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-$$

**Check the bonding at each chain carbon**

Look along the backbone. Every chain carbon is bonded to two neighbouring carbons plus two other atoms (H or $\text{CH}_3$). That is four sigma bonds and zero lone pairs.

That means:
$$\text{4 bonding pairs = sp}^3 \text{ hybridised = tetrahedral}$$

**Deduce the C-C-C angle**

A tetrahedral carbon has bond angles of about $109.5^{\circ}$, given as $109^{\circ}$ here. Since all the backbone carbons are $\text{sp}^3$, every C-C-C angle along the chain is the same.

options.A: Correct. All carbons in the poly(propene) backbone are sp3 tetrahedral with four single bonds, so all C-C-C angles are about 109 degrees.
options.B: Incorrect. This mixes up monomer and polymer. The 120 degree angle belongs to the sp2 C=C carbons in propene monomer, but that double bond is lost on polymerisation, so no 120 degree angles remain in the saturated chain.
options.C: Incorrect. Angles of 90 degrees and 180 degrees suggest octahedral or square planar geometry or a straight chain drawing. Polymer chains are drawn zig-zag on paper but the real 3D tetrahedral angle is still about 109 degrees.
options.D: Incorrect. 120 degrees is the trigonal planar angle for sp2 carbons in alkenes like propene. Students who forget that addition polymerisation converts C=C to C-C choose this trap.
